digest.intro: AI cracks 50-year math, the world's oil chokepoints are on fire.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz: Two Tankers Hit Mines, Iran Signals Control
items.blurb: Iran's IRGC says the tankers were transiting an 'unauthorized route' — framing the explosions as enforcement rather than incident. Simultaneously, the Houthis struck the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and a skyscraper in Riyadh, while Iran's VP dismissed any threat of a U.S. naval blockade. The energy infrastructure surrounding the Persian Gulf is now a live target system, not a backdrop.

items.title: Xi, Trump & Putin: First-Ever Trilateral Summit
items.blurb: The first trilateral meeting of its kind reshapes the optics of great-power alignment heading into 2027 — the three-way frame matters more than whatever communiqué emerges, because it normalizes a geometry that was unthinkable a decade ago. Watch what it does to European and Indo-Pacific posture in the weeks after.

items.title: ω = 9/4: The Matrix Multiplication Exponent Is Solved
items.blurb: Since Strassen showed in the late 1960s that you could multiply matrices faster than the naïve O(n³), the true exponent ω has been an open question — with most researchers betting on ω=2. This preprint claims to prove ω=9/4 exactly, both an upper and lower bound, meaning the answer is a clean rational number and the decades-long drift toward 2 was wrong. The lower bound is the genuinely shocking half: proving ω>2 was considered nearly as hard as P≠NP.

items.title: Scott Aaronson: 'Holy Shit' — What This Week's Math Actually Means
items.blurb: Aaronson was mid-dinner processing the VP≠VNP proof (itself following the Riemann Hypothesis proof from the week before) when the ω=9/4 lower bound dropped. His post is the clearest human-readable frame on what it means that AI systems are now proving not just hard theorems but lower bounds — a category of result that required fundamentally new structural insight, not just search. The Hubble analogy he lifts from his comments section — that we may have to accept proofs we can verify but not intuitively grasp, the way we accept telescope images — is the sentence that will stick.

items.title: Robin Sloan: Intellectual Telescopes
items.blurb: A short, generative post that lands exactly the right analogy for this week: AI-assisted proof isn't replacing mathematical sight, it's extending it the way Hubble extended human vision — you look at the picture it produces, in wonderment. Sloan sharpens it further by noting that the formal proof language Lean is as much the 'telescope' as the model; without it, there's nothing legible to verify or render for human understanding.

items.title: 'The Short Age of Dragon Riders' — A Physicist's Account of Working With AI
items.blurb: A theoretical physicist writes from inside the transition: since roughly August, models have passed the threshold where, 'in a proper harness,' they outperform most PhD physicists on day-to-day technical work. The honest observation is that the models still lack research taste — they execute beautifully on clear goals but can't yet generate good questions or find the creative leap out of a dead end. The essay's tension is that this is the rare window to be a 'dragon rider,' and it won't last long.

items.title: Voyager 1 Goes Silent at One Light-Day from Earth
items.blurb: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is now one light-day out — and has stopped sending science and engineering data, transmitting only a bare carrier wave. It's the third serious silence in recent years; the last was resolved by remotely diagnosing and bypassing a failed RAM chip across 24+ billion kilometers. The RTGs are running low, fuel lines have clogged, and nobody knows if it makes it to the 2030s — we may be in the last years of the most distant object humans have ever made.

items.title: Man a Machine — La Mettrie's 1749 First Edition
items.blurb: In 1747, physician Julien Offray de La Mettrie extended Descartes' 'animals are machines' claim to humans and was driven into exile — Calvinists, Catholics, and Lutherans briefly united just to persecute him. Frederick the Great gave him asylum and later delivered his funeral oration. The Public Domain Review surfaces the 1749 first edition in a week when AI systems are proving theorems that humans can verify but not fully grasp; La Mettrie's question — where exactly does the machine end and the mind begin — has never been more live.

facts.fact: The matrix multiplication exponent ω has been an open problem since 1969, when Strassen first showed it was less than 3 — this week's proof claims to settle it at exactly 9/4, a clean rational number most researchers did not expect.
Voyager 1 took 49 years to travel one light-day from Earth; a previous silence in 2023 was resolved by remotely diagnosing a single failed RAM chip from roughly 24 billion kilometers away.

When La Mettrie published 'Man a Machine' in 1747, Calvinists, Catholics, and Lutherans — otherwise divided over transubstantiation, free will, and papal infallibility — temporarily united to have him expelled from the Netherlands.

make_something.prompt: Build a small interface — physical or digital — that makes a proof or logical argument *feel* spatial rather than sequential. Inspired by the week's math breakthroughs and the Hubble analogy: a proof you can't follow line-by-line might still be navigable if rendered as a landscape. Try mapping a simple argument (even a syllogism) as a WebGL scene or a hand-drawn map where premises are terrain and conclusions are destinations. The constraint: no text labels — only geometry, color, and proximity carry the meaning.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film-essay that works like a generative system — images, memory, and time folded into each other through a narrator who keeps interrogating how images encode feeling. The 1983 sequences on Japan and Guinea sit next to meditations on video synthesis and the Zone Gede in ways that feel less like editing than like a mind thinking aloud. For someone who lives at the edge of physical and digital, Marker's obsession with what images actually *do* to consciousness is the right kind of rabbit hole.

art_picks.title: Every piece in the ongoing practice
art_picks.creator: Vera Molnár
art_picks.why: The Ur-source of generative 2D art — a painter who, starting in 1968, wrote her own programs to systematically disrupt geometric order and study what deviation feels like. Her work is the rare case where the system *is* the subject: she called her pre-computer method 'imaginary machine' and treated rule-breaking as the only honest form of self-expression. If you make generative 3D and want to understand what the tradition actually thought it was doing, Molnár is the starting point.

art_picks.title: Disintegration Loops
art_picks.creator: William Basinski
art_picks.why: Basinski discovered these while transferring 1980s tape loops to digital — the magnetic oxide flaked off in real time, and the recordings captured their own erasure. The result is 4+ hours of music that is literally a system destroying itself, structured by entropy rather than composition. The physical/digital threshold, the loop as form, the brutal beauty of irreversible process — it hits everything at once.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — Closing Days
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Freestanding screens in MoMA's Sculpture Garden generate hallucinatory images from fMRI brain scans — a neural network reconstructing human thought, mutated in real time by visitors' gazes and simulated cancer-cell data; it's a living system where human and machine cognition genuinely blur, and it closes Saturday.

events.name: Parker Ito & Evil Biscuit: Mint Condition — Opening
events.venue: Nguyen Wahed, 504 E 12th St, East Village
events.why: Parker Ito is one of the sharpest artists thinking about how networks, screens, and market systems shape what a painting even is — and Nguyen Wahed is the right gallery for it, a space that consistently treats digital and physical as the same material.

events.name: Technology, Consciousness, and Responsive Environment: Nora Khan on UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA, Floor T2, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Critic and theorist Nora Khan unpacks Huyghe's UUmwelt the day after the installation closes — a lecture on AI, responsive environments, and what it means to build a system that perceives; rare to get the critical reading this close to the work itself.

events.name: LCD Soundsystem
events.why: LCD's annual Brooklyn Steel residency is one of the few remaining live music rituals that still feels like a scene rather than a show — James Murphy's obsessive, loop-driven dance-punk hits different in the room where the band basically lives.

events.name: Arthur Jafa + Tyler Cowen in Conversation
events.why: Jafa makes films about Black visual culture as a system — compression, transmission, what images survive and why — and pairing him with an economist who thinks obsessively about culture and incentives is the kind of category-collision that actually generates new ideas.
